nameStory: Prickly lettuce gets its name from the small spines that line the underside of its leaf midribs and stems, making it feel rough and prickly to the touch. It's also called 'compass plant' because its leaves often twist to align north-south, helping the plant avoid the harsh midday sun while still catching morning and evening light.
description: Prickly lettuce is a tall, weedy annual or biennial plant that can grow 2-6 feet high with a spindly, branching appearance. It produces small yellow flowers in loose clusters and has deeply lobed leaves that often twist vertically. This European native has spread throughout New England as a common roadside weed and is actually the closest wild relative of our garden lettuce.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves that often twist to stand vertically (north-south orientation). Run your finger along the underside of the leaf midrib to feel the row of small, sharp prickles that give this plant its name.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale yellow dandelion-like flowers about half an inch across, clustered in loose, branching sprays at the top of the plant. Each flower head has only ray petals (no center disk).

idTips.label: Milky Sap
idTips.description: Break a leaf or stem to see thick, white, milky sap ooze out. This latex has a slightly unpleasant, fetid smell that's noticeable when you crush the plant.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white dandelion-like seed heads that blow apart in the wind. Each small brown seed has a feathery white parachute (pappus) attached.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and spindly with a single main stem that branches near the top into a loose, open flower cluster. Often grows in patches along disturbed ground.

habitat: Look for prickly lettuce in disturbed, sunny areas like roadsides, vacant lots, field edges, and waste ground throughout New England. It thrives in poor, compacted soils where many other plants struggle and is especially common along highways and in urban areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as low rosettes of deeply lobed leaves. First-year plants may remain as rosettes through their first season.
seasonality.summer: Mature plants bolt upward, producing their characteristic tall, branching stems topped with clusters of small yellow flowers from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen into fluffy white heads that disperse in autumn winds. Plants begin to die back after setting seed.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, but seeds overwinter in the soil. Biennial plants may persist as low rosettes under snow cover.

funFact: Prickly lettuce is like a living sundial - its leaves actually rotate throughout the day to track the sun's movement, and many orient themselves north-south to minimize water loss during hot midday hours, earning it the nickname 'compass plant' among early travelers.
confusionNotes: Don't confuse prickly lettuce with dandelions - dandelions have flowers on separate hollow stems and leaves that stay in a ground-level rosette. Prickly lettuce grows tall with flowers clustered at the top and has those distinctive prickles on the leaf undersides that dandelions lack.
contextualKnowledge: Be careful not to confuse this 'milk thistle' with the true milk thistle (Silybum marianum) used in herbal medicine - they're completely different plants that just happen to share a common name and milky sap.
compareHints: Prickly lettuce stands out from other wild lettuces by its prickly leaf undersides and the tendency for leaves to twist vertically. Canada wild lettuce is much taller (up to 10 feet) with smooth leaves, while tall blue lettuce has blue flowers instead of yellow. Hairy lettuce has fuzzy, hairy leaves rather than prickly ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the wild lettuces, tall blue lettuce stands out for its exceptional height and pale blue flowers - Canada wild lettuce has yellow blooms, while prickly lettuce has spiny leaves and is much shorter.
Canada wild lettuce differs from tall blue lettuce by its pale yellow flowers (versus blue), and from prickly lettuce by its smooth leaves without spines.

Among New England's wild lettuces, hairy lettuce is the fuzziest—literally! While tall blue lettuce is smooth-leaved and prickly lettuce has actual spines, hairy lettuce feels soft and downy to the touch.
Garden lettuce differs from its wild Lactuca relatives by having much broader, more tender leaves without the deeply cut or prickly edges found on species like prickly lettuce or Canada wild lettuce.
